### 💡 Codex Review Here are some automated review suggestions for this pull request. **Reviewed commit:** `b0ac7c15dc`
ℹ️ About Codex in GitHub
Codex has been enabled to automatically review pull requests in this repo. Reviews are triggered when you - Open a pull request for review - Mark a draft as ready - Comment "@codex review". If Codex has suggestions, it will comment; otherwise it will react with 👍. When you [sign up for Codex through ChatGPT](https://openai.com/codex), Codex can also answer questions or update the PR, like "@codex address that feedback".

Thanks for picking up #5804, a sliding TTL is the right fix: on main a session in use gets 404 at +25h, and your test fails there and passes here. A revoked or expired token still gets 401 with a live session, so a session that never goes idle still ends with its token.

One ask: `valid_mcp_session?` now writes to the cache (`app/controllers/mcp_controller.rb:232-234`), so the user check on `:232` is what stops it from rebinding another user's session. Please add a test next to `test/controllers/mcp_controller_test.rb:527`: user A initializes, user B sends A's session id with B's token, gets 404, and `Rails.cache.read("mcp:session:<id>")` still returns A's id.

Thanks, that test is the one. @KenTandrian a signed session id makes sense to me: auth already runs on every request through the Bearer token, so the id doesn't need storing, and a `message_verifier` id bound to the user closes both the idle and the cache-loss gaps while forged or cross-user ids still get 404. I'd do it in its own PR so this fix for sessions in use can land now. Clients should also re-initialize on that 404, which the spec requires.

Automated review pass (correctness-focused, no code changes made).

Checked `valid_mcp_session?`/`write_mcp_session` against both call sites (`prepare_mcp_request_context` for POST, and `method_not_allowed` for GET/DELETE): the TTL refresh only happens after the cache value matches the current request's authenticated user, so a forged, expired, or cross-user session id is rejected without extending its TTL — consistent with the new "another user cannot take over an MCP session id" test. No correctness issues found in this pass.

**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Refresh sessions for notification requests**

When a long-lived client sends session-bearing JSON-RPC notifications between normal calls, those requests never reach this refresh: `handle` returns `202` for every body without an `id` before `dispatch_jsonrpc` invokes `valid_mcp_session?` (the existing `notifications/initialized` path does exactly this). Consequently a client can send notifications within every 24-hour interval yet still have the session expire and receive a 404 on its next `tools/list`, so the sliding idle TTL is not refreshed on each use; validate and touch the session before the notification early return as well.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

Full details: Title check

**Explanation** The title names the change: the MCP session TTL is refreshed on each use. The raw summary and objectives confirm this is the main change, which adds sliding expiration for MCP sessions by rewriting the cache entry when a valid session ID is used. The title follows the conventional commit style and is specific enough for a teammate scanning history.
Full details: Linked Issues check

**Explanation** Only `#5804` is directly linked, and it is open. Its active-session requirement is met at head 708fb43. In app/controllers/mcp_controller.rb, valid_mcp_session? reads the cache entry, returns false on a missing entry or a user ID mismatch, and otherwise calls write_mcp_session. That call rewrites the entry with MCP_SESSION_TTL, so each valid request extends the expiry. Forged, expired, and cross-user IDs still return false, which produces 404. The head change since the previous review adds only a guard ordering (the read check runs before the write) and a cross-user test. It does not change the expiry logic. The new tests cover active use at +20h and +40h (200), idle expiry after a full TTL (404), and cross-user rejection with the cached owner unchanged. Remaining gaps are accepted scope limits stated in the PR and objectives: sessions idle for more than one day still expire, and sessions still live only in Rails.cache, so a cache flush or restart drops them. The issue's stateless signed-ID approach is not implemented. The issue offers a sliding cache TTL as an acceptable alternative, so this does not fail the requirement. Test results are author-reported; this review did not run the suite.
Full details: Out of Scope Changes check

**Explanation** The whole-PR diff (merge base e0d9c9c to head 708fb43) touches two files. app/controllers/mcp_controller.rb adds write_mcp_session, which centralizes the cache write used by handle_initialize and valid_mcp_session?. It also adds the sliding refresh in valid_mcp_session?. Both changes implement the sliding-expiry requirement of `#5804`. test/controllers/mcp_controller_test.rb adds three tests: active use past the original TTL, cross-user session takeover rejection, and the existing idle-expiry case. These tests verify the behavior of `#5804` and the cross-user requirement in the issue's expected behavior. No unrelated changes were found. The test fixture users(:family_member) was not checked in this review.

Thanks for picking up #5804! I am the issue reporter.

Two quick concerns before this closes the issue:

1. **24h idle expiry:** Keeping `MCP_SESSION_TTL = 1.day` means any long-lived MCP client idle for >24h still hits `404 Invalid MCP session id` (whereas Doorkeeper tokens live `1.year` and web `Session`s use `30.days`).
2. **Cache-only storage:** Since `McpController` only stores `mcp_user.id` and already enforces Bearer auth per request, relying on `Rails.cache` still drops sessions on Redis restarts/evictions, `:memory_store` without `REDIS_URL`, and local dev (`:null_store`).

I'm thinking it might be cleaner to move `Mcp-Session-Id` to a stateless HMAC-signed token (`Rails.application.message_verifier(:mcp_session)` binding `{ s, u }` to `mcp_user.id`) — either here or in a separate PR — which avoids both gaps while still returning `404` on forged/tampered/cross-user IDs. Alternatively, bumping `MCP_SESSION_TTL` to `30.days` (matching `Session::INACTIVITY_TIMEOUT`) would at least cover the idle window if we'd rather stay on `Rails.cache`.

@dgilperez @jjmata let me know what you think!

Added the test next to the invalid-session one: user A initializes, user B sends A's session id with B's own token, gets 404, and the cache entry still holds A's id. With the user comparison removed from `valid_mcp_session?` the test fails (200 instead of 404).
